blocks.text: Scenario A — Counselling
A 32-year-old woman with persistent high-risk HPV has been referred for colposcopy. Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Scenario B — Practical station
Demonstrate how you would perform a colposcopic examination of the cervix.
Scenario C — Image interpretation
A woman with an abnormal cervical smear has a dense acetowhite lesion with coarse mosaicism. Describe the findings and discuss their significance.
Scenario D — Biopsy interpretation
Colposcopy-guided biopsy demonstrates CIN 3. Explain the diagnosis and management options.
Scenario E — Unsatisfactory colposcopy
The transformation zone cannot be fully visualised. Explain the implications and further management.
Colposcopy is the examination of the cervix, and sometimes the vagina and vulva, using a colposcope that provides magnification and illumination.

blocks.text: The colposcope remains outside the vagina. A speculum is inserted to visualise the cervix.
Before interpreting colposcopy images, understand the anatomy.
The part of the cervix projecting into the vagina. It is predominantly covered by stratified squamous epithelium.
The canal extending through the cervix, lined predominantly by columnar glandular epithelium.
The junction between squamous and columnar epithelium.
The region between the original and current squamocolumnar junctions where squamous metaplasia occurs.
Most cervical precancerous lesions arise in the transformation zone.

content_groups.group_title: Why is the transformation zone important?

items.text: It is the principal site where most cervical precancers develop.
Its location changes with age, hormonal status and pregnancy.
It may be fully visible or extend into the endocervical canal.
If the entire transformation zone or upper limit of a lesion cannot be visualised, the examination may be inadequate for confidently excluding more significant disease.
Abnormal cervical cytology, especially high-grade abnormalities.
High-risk HPV positivity requiring referral under the relevant screening pathway.
Persistent HPV infection with concerning screening history.
A clinically suspicious cervical lesion.
Unexplained persistent postcoital bleeding or other concerning symptoms after appropriate assessment.
Follow-up after selected treatments for cervical precancer.
Evaluation of suspected cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.

blocks.text: A woman with a suspicious visible lesion requires diagnostic assessment regardless of a previous negative screening result.

content_groups.group_title: When is colposcopy not simply a routine screening procedure?

blocks.text: Colposcopy is a diagnostic assessment, not a substitute for routine screening in all eligible women. A normal colposcopic appearance also does not automatically negate a high-risk screening result; management depends on the entire clinical picture.
This section is important in a practical OSCE.

items.text: Introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity.
Explain why colposcopy has been recommended.
Ask about previous screening results and relevant cervical procedures.
Establish whether the patient may be pregnant.
Explain that the examination involves a speculum and may include application of solutions and cervical biopsy.
Discuss possible discomfort, light bleeding and the possibility of an inadequate examination.
Obtain informed consent.
Offer a chaperone.
Provide privacy for undressing and positioning.
Prepare the colposcope, speculum, appropriate solutions, biopsy forceps, specimen containers and documentation.

blocks.text: A patient can ask for the procedure to pause or stop at any time.

"The examination allows us to look closely at your cervix using a magnifying instrument. We may apply a dilute solution to highlight abnormal areas, and if needed, take a small tissue sample for laboratory testing. You may feel pressure or brief discomfort, and a biopsy can cause a small amount of bleeding. You can ask me to pause or stop at any point. Do you have any questions before we begin?"

In an OSCE, explain the steps in order and demonstrate the relevant actions using the equipment provided. In clinical practice, the examination and any biopsy must be performed by a trained clinician.

blocks.text: A grossly suspicious lesion should be documented and assessed appropriately; do not delay referral while attempting to classify it as a routine precancer.
Saline may help remove mucus and assess surface and vascular patterns. The clinician can examine the cervix at low and higher magnification.
Dilute acetic acid is commonly used to highlight abnormal epithelium.
Areas with increased nuclear density may become white, producing an acetowhite reaction.

blocks.text: Acetowhitening is not specific to CIN; inflammation, immature metaplasia and other conditions can also produce whitening.

content_groups.group_title: Step 6 — Apply Lugol's iodine if indicated

blocks.text: Lugol's iodine stains glycogen-rich mature squamous epithelium dark brown.
Abnormal epithelium with reduced glycogen uptake may remain yellow or mustard-coloured.
Iodine-negative areas are not automatically precancerous, because immature metaplasia and columnar epithelium may also fail to stain.

content_groups.group_title: Step 7 — Take a targeted biopsy if indicated

items.text: Identify the most suspicious areas.
Take directed biopsies according to the clinical indication and local protocol.
Label each specimen accurately.
Arrange histopathological examination.

blocks.text: Endocervical sampling may be indicated when the transformation zone is not fully visible or when glandular disease is suspected, but the technique and whether it is appropriate depend on the clinical situation. Endocervical curettage must not be performed during pregnancy.

items.text: Assess whether the entire SCJ and lesion are visible.
Record the transformation-zone type and lesion characteristics.
Remove the speculum gently.
Explain aftercare and when results are expected.
Ensure a follow-up appointment or recall system is in place.

blocks.text: A. Normal appearance
Smooth, regular epithelium without suspicious focal changes. The SCJ may be visible depending on the transformation-zone type.
Interpretation: no obvious colposcopic lesion, but screening history and adequacy still determine management.
B. Cervical ectropion
Red, velvety columnar epithelium around the external os.
Interpretation: often benign and may cause contact bleeding. Investigate symptoms and atypical features rather than assuming every red cervix is ectropion.
C. Thin acetowhite epithelium
Faint whitening after acetic acid, sometimes with fine vascular patterns.
Interpretation: may be associated with low-grade changes, but the appearance is not diagnostic on its own.
D. Dense acetowhite epithelium
Thick, opaque whitening with distinct margins; coarse mosaic or punctation may be present.
Interpretation: raises concern for high-grade disease and warrants appropriate biopsy or other guideline-directed assessment.
E. Suspicious invasive lesion
Irregular, ulcerated or exophytic mass, contact bleeding or atypical vessels.
Interpretation: urgent diagnostic assessment and biopsy are required. Avoid ablative treatment of a lesion in which invasion is suspected.

blocks.text: No single feature proves CIN 2, CIN 3 or invasive cancer. Histopathology and clinical context determine the diagnosis.

content_groups.group_title: What if the transformation zone is not fully visible?

blocks.text: An incompletely visible transformation zone is not itself a diagnosis of cancer. However, it can make it difficult to exclude significant disease.
Management depends on the screening result, age, risk factors, suspected lesion and local guideline. Options may include additional sampling, diagnostic excision or specialist review.
The biopsy result is central to management.

rows: Follow the pathway appropriate to the screening history and adequacy of the examination
Often surveillance rather than immediate treatment
Individualised assessment; treatment is common, while surveillance may be suitable in selected patients
Usually treated because of the risk of progression
Specialist assessment and appropriate diagnostic excision or other management
Refer for staging and cancer management

items.text: LLETZ/LEEP: removes the transformation zone and provides tissue for histology.
Cone biopsy: removes a cone-shaped portion of the cervix and may be indicated for glandular disease or suspected microinvasion.
Ablation: suitable only for carefully selected lesions when eligibility criteria are met and invasion has been excluded.
Surveillance: appropriate for selected lower-risk lesions, with reliable follow-up.

There are no suspicious acetowhite lesions, abnormal vascular patterns or visible masses. The colposcopic appearance is normal. Management will be guided by the referral cytology, HPV result and previous screening history."

content_groups.group_title: Example 2 — Findings suggestive of low-grade disease

blocks.text: "There is a small area of thin acetowhite epithelium near the transformation zone, without coarse vascular abnormalities or features suspicious for invasion. The appearance may be consistent with low-grade disease. A biopsy will be taken if indicated by the referral findings and clinical assessment."

content_groups.group_title: Example 3 — Findings suggestive of high-grade disease

blocks.text: "There is a well-demarcated, dense acetowhite lesion involving the transformation zone, with coarse mosaicism. The appearance is suspicious for high-grade cervical intraepithelial disease. Directed biopsy and histopathological assessment are required."

"The cervix contains an irregular, friable lesion with contact bleeding and abnormal vascularity. The appearance is suspicious for invasive cervical malignancy. I would arrange urgent specialist assessment and tissue diagnosis, avoiding ablative treatment."

"The squamocolumnar junction is not fully visualised, consistent with a type 3 transformation zone. The examination is inadequate to exclude disease in the unseen endocervical region. Further assessment will be guided by the referral result and risk profile."

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is colposcopy?
Magnified examination of the cervix, usually after application of acetic acid and sometimes iodine, to identify abnormal epithelium and guide biopsy.
Q2. Why is acetic acid applied?
It causes abnormal epithelium with increased nuclear density to appear white. The reaction helps identify suspicious areas but is not diagnostic by itself.
Q3. Why does abnormal epithelium fail to stain with iodine?
It may contain less glycogen than mature squamous epithelium. However, iodine-negative areas are not necessarily precancerous.
Q4. What is the difference between punctation and mosaicism?
Punctation describes red dots formed by vascular loops viewed end-on. Mosaicism describes a network of vessels surrounding epithelial blocks. Coarse patterns are more concerning than fine patterns.
Q5. What does a type 3 transformation zone mean?
The transformation zone extends into the endocervical canal and the SCJ is not completely visible, potentially limiting the examination.
Q6. Can colposcopy alone confirm CIN 3?
No. Colposcopy estimates the likelihood and extent of disease. Histopathological examination of tissue is required to establish the diagnosis when biopsy is indicated.
Q7. What should you do if you suspect invasive cancer?
Arrange urgent specialist diagnostic assessment and biopsy. Do not use routine ablative treatment for a lesion suspicious for invasion.
Q8. Is colposcopy safe during pregnancy?

Colposcopy can be performed when indicated. Biopsy may be undertaken if clinically necessary, but treatment of precancer is generally deferred until after pregnancy unless cancer is suspected. Endocervical curettage is contraindicated.
Q9. What is LLETZ?
Large loop excision of the transformation zone, also called LEEP in some settings, removes abnormal cervical tissue using an electrically heated wire loop.
Q10. What are the complications of a cervical biopsy?
Usually mild discomfort, spotting or bleeding. Infection is uncommon. Significant bleeding requires clinical assessment.

items.text: Colposcopy is a diagnostic examination, not a screening test.
The transformation zone is the principal site of most cervical precancers.
Acetic acid highlights suspicious epithelium, but acetowhitening is not specific for CIN.
Histopathology establishes the tissue diagnosis.
A suspicious invasive lesion requires biopsy and specialist assessment, not ablation.

blocks.text: Exam practice
A 34-year-old woman is referred for colposcopy after HSIL cytology. Examination shows a dense acetowhite lesion with coarse mosaicism. The upper limit of the lesion is not fully visible.
What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?
The lesion is definitely benign because the cervix is not ulcerated.
The findings are suspicious for high-grade disease; obtain appropriate tissue diagnosis and assess whether diagnostic excision is needed because the lesion is not fully visible.
Diagnose invasive cervical cancer without biopsy.
Perform ablative treatment immediately without further assessment.
